By
Terrence Hill
Published: Nov 24 2026, 5:17 AM EST
Share on Facebook

Sierra ai
Sierra, the AI customer service company co-founded by OpenAI board chair Bret Taylor and former Google executive Clay Bavor, said Monday it is raising $1.75 billion at a $30 billion valuation, roughly 75 times its more than $400 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). That multiple only holds if Sierra's outcome-based pricing, which charges customers when an AI agent resolves a conversation rather than for the compute it burns, produces revenue that lasts. Anyone weighing AI customer service contracts, or judging whether private AI valuations are tracking real revenue, needs to understand that bet.
Greenoaks and Lightspeed are leading the round, and Benchmark, Sequoia, GV and Tiger Global are investing more. Sierra's own announcement says it is "raising" the money, while TechCrunch reported the round as raised, so the funds may not all have closed.
Valuation Doubled in Six Months While Revenue Also Doubled
The $30 billion figure is about twice the "more than $15 billion" valuation Sierra carried when it raised $950 million in May , led by Tiger Global and GV. Revenue grew about as fast: Sierra reported $200 million in ARR in May and more than $400 million by October 30, and it says the third quarter alone added more than $150 million.
That makes the multiple compress, not inflate. At the $10 billion valuation, TechCrunch cited a 100x revenue multiple on $100 million in ARR. Using the $15.8 billion figure reported for the May round, Sierra was priced near 79 times ARR, and it sits near 75 times now.

May 2026 $15.8 billion (reported) $200 million About 79 times
November 2026 $30 billion More than $400 million About 75 times
How Per-Outcome Billing Moves Inference Cost Onto Sierra
Traditional software bills per seat. Many AI vendors bill for usage, meaning the tokens a model processes, which passes the cost of running the model to the customer. Sierra instead charges when its agent completes a task such as resolving a support request, and says an unresolved conversation usually means no charge . The logical consequence is that Sierra, not the customer, absorbs the inference cost of every conversation the agent fails to resolve. That is an analysis of the pricing model, not a figure Sierra has disclosed, and Sierra has not published its gross margin.
Sierra's engineering answer is to route each conversation through a constellation of more than 15 models , with its own fine-tuned models handling some steps, rather than one large model. Its tooling includes Agent OS 2.0 .
The cost pressure is industrywide. ICONIQ's State of AI snapshot tracks average gross margins for AI products rising from 41% in 2024 to 45% in 2025, with a projected 52% in 2026, against 70% to 85% for classic software . Sierra's per-outcome model makes reliability a margin issue: every failed attempt costs compute with no revenue attached.
Reliability is measurable. Sierra's own τ-bench benchmark scores agents on repeated attempts at the same task, using a metric called pass^k, the probability that all k attempts succeed. In the 2024 τ-bench paper , GPT-4o completed fewer than half of tasks and scored under 25% on pass^8 in the retail domain. Those results are from 2024 and from Sierra's own benchmark, not an independent audit, and Sierra has not published current figures for its production agents.
Attribution is the other hard problem. Sierra's own June 2026 Outcomemaxxing post says outcome pricing is more complex than seat or consumption pricing operationally, contractually and in accounting terms. That is why the largest unstated question in this deal is whether "ARR" means the same thing for an outcome-priced company as for a seat-based one. ARR is a company-reported run-rate, and neither GAAP nor IFRS defines it , so a figure built on per-outcome fees can move with conversation volume and with how outcomes are defined in each contract.
Read more:
AI Agent Economics: Token Tax Locks Gross Margins 30 Points Below SaaS Baseline
Is 75 Times Revenue High Compared With Harvey, Fin and Decagon?
It is the highest multiple among the comparable deals below, though some rivals are close or cannot be compared cleanly. Harvey was valued at $15.6 billion on about $400 million in ARR, roughly 39 times; Harvey's own blog gives $15.5 billion. Decagon, valued at $4.5 billion in January , said in August its annualized revenue passed $100 million , about 45 times. Parloa, valued at $3 billion in January , reported more than $50 million in ARR in December 2025, about 60 times. Wonderful raised $550 million at a $5 billion valuation in September, and Calcalist estimated its run rate at $70 million, about 71 times.
Salesforce's $3.6 billion deal for Intercom's Fin, which closed September 10 , looks cheap by comparison at about 9 times a reported $400 million in ARR. But roughly $300 million of that is reported to be legacy software revenue, and only about $100 million is the Fin AI agent itself, which implies a multiple of up to 36 times on the AI portion.
Analysts quoted so far say the price needs more than headline growth. One analysis says the May valuation should not rest on revenue alone , and another names net revenue retention on Fortune 50 accounts as the diligence item that matters. Applied Digital Secures 18-Year AI Data Center Lease Worth $5.4 Billion
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 7:08 AM
Applied Digital Secures 18-Year AI Data Center Lease Worth $5.4 Billion
Applied Digital has signed an 18-year lease with a tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler for 150 megawatts of critical information-technology capacity.
The agreement represents approximately $5.4 billion in contracted base-term revenue. Potential revenue could reach approximately $12.7 billion if the customer exercises every renewal option, extending the total term to 33 years.
The latest agreement increases Applied Digital’s total contracted base-term lease revenue to more than $41 billion. That figure could approach $100 billion if customers exercise all available renewal options.
Growing Contracted AI Infrastructure Portfolio
Applied Digital said the latest lease contains higher pricing and improved commercial terms compared with its earlier agreements.
Its contracted portfolio now represents more than 1.6 gigawatts of critical IT load and 2.2 gigawatts of grid-connected peak load.
Approximately 75% of contracted base-term lease revenue is attributable to investment-grade customers, strengthening the credit profile of the company’s long-term revenue base.
Delivery of the newly leased capacity is expected to begin during the first half of 2028, subject to development milestones, utility arrangements and regulatory approvals.
Applied Digital plans to finance construction through equity already committed from its balance sheet and its $5 billion programmatic partnership with Macquarie Asset Management. Project financing supported by the hyperscaler lease is expected to follow.
The company expects to complete the remaining project financing for Delta Forge 1 and Polaris Forge 3 during the first quarter of 2027. Financing for Delta Forge 2 is expected in the second quarter.
KEY QUOTES:
“Securing another large-scale, long-term lease with a tier-one investment-grade hyperscaler reinforces to us the strength of our customer relationships and the quality of our contracted revenue. We believe our portfolio reflects the scale and sophistication of the infrastructure we’ve developed, and our focus remains on executing with the speed, discipline and consistency required for our customers.”
Wes Cummins, Chairman And CEO Of Applied Digital
“This approach is designed to optimize our cost of capital while aligning capital deployment with construction timelines.”
Saidal Mohmand, CFO Of Applied Digital

DICK’S Sporting Goods Reports $5.13 Billion in Q3 Sales, Raises Full-Year Earnings Outlook
November 24, 2026
DICK’S Sporting Goods, Inc. (NYSE: DKS) reported third-quarter fiscal 2026 net sales of $5.13 billion, an increase of 23.2% year over year, as its core sporting goods business delivered continued comparable sales growth and its acquired Foot Locker operations showed signs of improvement.
For the quarter ended October 31, 2026, consolidated net income increased 114% to $161 million from $75 million in the prior-year period. Diluted earnings per share increased 117% to $1.87 from $0.86.
On an adjusted basis, however, net income declined 7% to $168 million, while diluted earnings per share decreased 6% to $1.94 from $2.07 a year earlier.
Consolidated operating margin increased to 4.7% from 2.2%, while adjusted operating margin declined to 4.9% from 5.8%.
The year-over-year sales comparison reflects a full quarter of Foot Locker operations, compared with approximately eight weeks in the prior-year period following the September 2025 acquisition.
The DICK’S Business generated third-quarter net sales of $3.34 billion, compared with $3.24 billion a year earlier. Comparable sales increased 2.6%, supported by a strong back-to-school shopping season, while segment operating income reached $290.6 million.
The Foot Locker Business generated $1.80 billion in quarterly net sales and recorded an operating loss of $40.9 million. Pro forma comparable sales increased 0.5%, compared with a decline of 4.7% in the prior-year quarter.
Foot Locker’s North American comparable sales increased 1.3%, while international comparable sales declined 1.8%. Comparable sales at the U.S. Foot Locker banner increased more than 4%.
“Our third quarter performance was driven by another strong quarter in the DICK’S Business, which continues to benefit from the breadth and flexibility of our portfolio,” said Ed Stack , Executive Chairman of DICK’S Sporting Goods. “We’re gaining market share, and we’re very confident in our competitive position.”
The company continued investing in its experiential retail concepts, opening six House of Sport locations and three DICK’S Field House locations during the quarter. The expansion brought its nationwide footprint to 47 House of Sport and 55 Field House locations.
GameChanger, the company’s digital youth sports platform, marked its tenth anniversary as part of DICK’S, with full-year fiscal 2026 revenue expected to approach $200 million.
“We’re continuing to invest behind our long-term growth opportunities,” said Lauren Hobart , President and Chief Executive Officer of DICK’S Sporting Goods. “House of Sport has delivered strong sales, profitability and returns, while GameChanger continues to scale and deepen our relationship with millions of youth athletes and families.”
DICK’S repurchased 6.7 million shares of common stock for $903 million during the third quarter, bringing year-to-date share repurchases to approximately $1.04 billion. The company had $2.12 billion remaining under its existing share repurchase authorization at quarter-end.
The board also declared a quarterly cash dividend of $1.25 per share, payable December 24, 2026, to shareholders of record on December 11, 2026.
For the first nine months of fiscal 2026, consolidated net sales increased 44.6% to $15.88 billion, while net income increased 10% to $796 million. Adjusted net income declined 8% to $748 million.
Following its third-quarter performance, DICK’S raised its full-year consolidated diluted earnings guidance to $11.40 to $12.25 per share, compared with its previous forecast of $10.94 to $11.94.
Adjusted diluted earnings guidance increased to $11.45 to $12.30 per share, from the previous range of $11.00 to $12.00.
The company expects full-year consolidated net sales of $22 billion to $22.2 billion and operating income of $1.47 billion to $1.56 billion.
For its core DICK’S Business, the company raised the lower end of its comparable sales outlook, now projecting growth of 3.3% to 4.0%, with segment operating income expected to reach $1.56 billion to $1.61 billion.
Foot Locker’s full-year expectations remain unchanged, with projected net sales of $7.4 billion to $7.5 billion, pro forma comparable sales ranging from a 2% decline to flat growth, and an anticipated operating loss of $40 million to $80 million.
DICK’S completed its $2.5 billion acquisition of Foot Locker on September 8, 2025, significantly expanding its international retail presence and athletic footwear portfolio.
As part of the integration, the company continues to optimize inventory, close underperforming stores and restructure acquired assets. It has incurred $520 million in related pre-tax charges to date and expects total charges of up to $750 million.
As of October 31, 2026, DICK’S operated 3,097 company-owned retail locations across its DICK’S and Foot Locker businesses, with an additional 271 licensed Foot Locker stores internationally.

AI Funding Boom: Mumbai Overtakes Bengaluru as Indian AI Startups Raise $1.6 Billion in 2026
India's artificial intelligence startup ecosystem is seeing a big jump in investor interest, with funding nearly doubling in the first nine months of 2026. But the money is not flowing evenly across …
Published By :
Business Desk , The Open Press
Last Updated: November 24, 2026, 19:52 IST
Artificial intelligence themed illustration. Indian AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding between January and September 2026, nearly double the amount raised a year earlier.
India's artificial intelligence startup ecosystem is seeing a big jump in investor interest, with funding nearly doubling in the first nine months of 2026. But the money is not flowing evenly across the country, and a handful of cities are attracting most of the investments.
Indian AI companies raised $1.6 billion in equity funding between January and September 2026, a 96 percent increase from the $822 million raised during the same period last year. The latest figures also mark a 162 percent jump from the $616 million raised in the corresponding period of 2024, according to Tracxn's India AI 9M 2026 Report.
Mumbai emerged as the country's biggest AI funding hub, followed by Bengaluru and Chennai. Together, the three cities accounted for around 96 percent of all AI investments raised in India during the period.
Mumbai takes the lead
Mumbai has emerged as the biggest destination for AI investments, overtaking Bengaluru in the first nine months of 2026.
AI companies based in Mumbai raised $765 million during the period, accounting for 48 percent of the total funding raised in the country. This is a sharp increase from the $15.7 million raised in the same period last year, when the city accounted for just 2 percent of India's AI funding.
A couple of large deals played a major role in this jump. Mumbai-based AI cloud provider Neysa raised $600 million in a Series B round in February, making it the largest AI funding deal in the country during the period. The round alone accounted for around 37 percent of India's total AI funding. Another major deal came from Yotta, which raised $150 million in a Series D round in July.
Bengaluru second, Chennai third
Bengaluru, long known as India's startup capital, secured the second position with $711 million in AI funding. The city accounted for 44 percent of the total investments, down from 54 percent in the first nine months of 2025.
Several large deals contributed to Bengaluru's funding numbers. Generative AI startup Sarvam raised $255 million in a Series B round in June and another $90.4 million in August. Emergent was among the other prominent companies that attracted investor interest.
Chennai took the third spot, with AI companies raising $75.5 million, accounting for around 5 percent of the country's total funding. Most of this came from Freehand, which raised $75 million in a Series B round.
Bigger cheques, fewer deals
While the total amount raised by Indian AI companies has increased sharply, the number of funding rounds has moved in the opposite direction.
The sector recorded 87 funding rounds in the first nine months of 2026, down 42 percent from 149 in the same period last year. At the same time, the average deal size increased to $18.5 million from $5.5 million. This suggests that investors are putting larger amounts of money into fewer companies rather than spreading their investments across a wider pool of startups.
The trend is also visible in the biggest deals. The ten largest funding rounds together raised $1.5 billion, accounting for 90 percent of the total AI funding during the period.
Early-stage funding jumped 191 percent to $1.3 billion from $434 million a year ago. Early-stage deals accounted for 78 percent of the total funding, compared with 53 percent in the first nine months of 2025. Late-stage funding increased by a modest 4 percent to $280 million, while seed-stage investments declined 42 percent to $69.2 million.
Three new AI unicorns in 2026
The funding momentum also helped India add three new AI unicorns in the first nine months of 2026. Neysa, Sarvam and Emergent crossed the $1 billion valuation mark during this period, compared with one new AI unicorn in the corresponding period last year.
However, the number of investors backing Indian AI companies declined. A total of 111 investors participated in funding rounds during the period, down 34 percent from 169 a year earlier. First-time investors also fell 39 percent to 43.
Among early-stage investors, Peak XV Partners led with three investments, followed by Prosus and Khosla Ventures with two each. Antler, IvyCap Ventures and Finvolve were among the leading seed-stage investors.
On the exits front, Indian AI companies recorded six acquisitions, compared with five in the first nine months of 2025. However, there were no public listings during the period.
Despite the sharp increase in domestic investments, India's share of global AI funding remains relatively small. Worldwide, AI companies raised $383.5 billion in the first nine months of 2026. India's $1.6 billion contribution accounted for just 0.4 percent of the global total, placing it ninth among countries.
Key points
- Indian AI companies raised $1.6 billion between January and September 2026, up 96 percent from $822 million a year earlier, as per Tracxn. - Mumbai led with $765 million, or 48 percent of the total, overtaking Bengaluru, which raised $711 million. - Chennai was third with $75.5 million. Why it matters
South-east Asian payment firms secured US$1.6 billion by mid-November 2026, driven almost entirely by mega-rounds for Ant International and Airwallex.
Capital concentration in Singapore starves early-stage regional fintechs, with deal counts collapsing to 10 and seed transactions tumbling from nine to one.

Retail News Asia newsroom analysis
South-east Asia’s payment companies raised US$1.6 billion in equity funding between Jan 1 and Nov 17, 2026. That total more than doubles the US$733 million secured across the entire twelve months of 2025.
The capital injection represents the highest annual funding level for the sector since 2022. It extends a three-year recovery from 2023, when sector investment hit a trough of US$270 million. Capital flow, however, concentrated heavily into a tiny cluster of mega-transactions rather than a broad market expansion.
Mega-rounds skew early-stage totals
Two transactions accounted for the vast majority of the capital raised across the region this year. Ant International secured US$1.2 billion in a Series A round in July, while cross-border payments provider Airwallex closed a US$320 million Series H round in June.

Because Ant International structured its transaction as a Series A round, early-stage capital metrics surged to US$1.3 billion for the year. Late-stage funding reached just US$320 million through mid-November. The breakdown reverses the distribution recorded in 2025, when late-stage financing rounds comprised US$662 million of the US$733 million raised.
Deal volumes fall across the region
Underlying deal activity contracted sharply despite the top-line dollar expansion. Investors completed only 10 equity deals across South-east Asia through Nov 17, 2026.
Early-stage venture creation experienced the steepest drop. Seed rounds fell from nine completed transactions in 2025 to a single deal in 2026. The compression leaves early-stage fintech founders facing a substantially narrower base of active institutional checks than in prior fundraising cycles.
Singapore captures the bulk of capital
Geographic allocation remains skewed toward Singapore, which drew approximately 71.1 per cent of all payment sector funding in South-east Asia. The city-state has payment unicorns Airwallex, Coda, and cross-border infrastructure network Thunes.
Thunes represents the most recent addition to the regional unicorn roster, having crossed the US$1 billion valuation mark in April 2025. Other markets maintain discrete domestic champions: Thailand houses Omise and Ascend Money, Indonesia supports Xendit, the Philippines counts GCash and Voyager Innovations, and Vietnam includes MoMo and VNPay.
Trade sales dominate liquidity events
Trade acquisitions continue to serve as the primary route to liquidity for investors and founders in the region. South-east Asia has logged 53 acquisitions and nine initial public offerings in the payments vertical to date.
The path to an acquisition remains extended. Payment firms averaged 19.5 years from their initial funding round to an acquisition, securing an average transaction price of US$80.9 million. Corporate buyers completed two acquisitions in 2026 through Nov 17, compared with three in 2025, while public listings remained flat with one IPO completed in each year.
What this means
Headline funding gains mask a severe liquidity crunch for South-east Asian fintech. Funnelling capital into Ant International and Airwallex creates an unsustainable divide. This lopsided backing directly pressures regional champions like Xendit, GCash, and MoMo, which must now defend domestic turf without comparable mega-checks. While Thunes secured a unicorn valuation in April 2025, newer entrants face a closed door after seed activity collapsed to a solitary round. The core risk is an innovation drought across peripheral markets as Singapore monopolises institutional dry powder. Watch whether corporate acquirers surpass the US$80.9 million average exit price before year-end.

The remaining $265 million is being provided through the International Finance Corporation (IFC) to support the private sector in the DRC.
The financing will support small and medium-sized enterprises, mining subcontracting, local processing of resources and trade finance.
President Felix Tshisekedi used the opening ceremony to reaffirm the DRC’s aim to move beyond extracting resources to creating added value through local processing, saying this would bring “lasting prosperity for the people.”

Telangana tech ecosystem raises $726M in equity funding in 9M 2026
November
24,
2026
Telangana’s technology ecosystem attracted $726 million in equity funding during the first nine months of 2026 (9M 2026), marking a 266% increase from $199 million in the corresponding period last year. However, the surge in funding was driven largely by a handful of large transactions, particularly a $423 million Series B round by Hyderabad-based data centre company CtrlS.
According to Tracxn Technologies’ Telangana Tech – 9M 2026 Report, funding during January–September 2026 was also 12% higher than the $647 million raised in the corresponding period of 2024. However, the number of funding rounds declined 30% to 73 from 105 a year ago, indicating a concentration of capital in fewer, larger deals.
The average funding round size increased to $9.9 million from $1.9 million in 9M 2025. CtrlS, which raised a total of $451 million through two rounds during the period, accounted for a significant share of the funding inflow.
CtrlS leads funding surge, top 10 deals account for 91% of capital
The 10 largest funding rounds accounted for $664 million, or 91% of Telangana’s total technology funding during 9M 2026.
CtrlS’s $423 million Series B round in June, backed by CPP Investments, was the largest transaction of the period. The round alone represented 58% of total funding and 80% of the $527 million increase over the year-ago period. The company had also raised $28.2 million in a Series A round in February. Other significant transactions included a $60 million Series C round by space launch company Skyroot Aerospace in May and a $50 million Series B round by Edubuk in March.
Meanwhile, Series A and later-stage funding rounds declined 18% to 23 from 28. The number of first-time funded companies also fell 31% to 20 from 29.
Early-stage funding jumps 334% to $622 million
Early-stage investments accounted for the bulk of funding, rising 334% to $622 million from $143 million in 9M 2025. The segment contributed 86% of total funding during the period, although the number of early-stage rounds declined 27% to 19.
The CtrlS Series B transaction alone accounted for 68% of early-stage funding. Late-stage funding increased 426% to $78.1 million from $14.8 million, with four rounds compared with two in the year-ago period. However, it remained 84% below the $482 million raised in 9M 2024. In contrast, seed-stage funding declined 35% to $26.4 million, accounting for just 4% of the total. The number of seed rounds also fell 35% to 50 from 77.
Investor participation weakened during the period. The number of active investors declined 22% to 61 from 78. International investors fell 43% to 13 from 23, while first-time investors dropped 36% to 30 from 47.
Among investors, Aum Ventures and V3 Ventures made two seed-stage investments each. Prosus led early-stage investors with two investments in Equal and Deccan AI.
Enterprise infrastructure attracts $454 million
Enterprise infrastructure emerged as the largest-funded technology segment, attracting $454 million in 9M 2026, nearly 35 times the $13 million raised in the corresponding period last year. The segment accounted for 63% of Telangana’s total technology funding.
Enterprise applications ranked second, attracting $142 million, up 79% from $79.4 million in 9M 2025. Aerospace, maritime and defence technology companies raised $78.5 million, a 445% increase from $14.4 million a year earlier.
Hyderabad accounted for the entire funding raised by Telangana-based technology companies during the period, compared with 98% in 9M 2025, underlining the city’s dominance in the state’s startup ecosystem.
Acquisitions decline to six; DSPL records sole IPO
Exit activity remained subdued, with acquisitions declining to six in 9M 2026 from nine in the year-ago period, although the number was higher than the five acquisitions recorded in 9M 2024.
IncNut Digital’s acquisition by Emami for $33.9 million in May was the only deal with a disclosed transaction value. The other five acquisitions had undisclosed financial details. These included Perspect’s acquisition by Unstop and Alteons Energy’s acquisition by Sanmar Group, both in September. No acquirer completed more than one deal during the period.
Telangana recorded one public listing during 9M 2026, compared with none in 9M 2025. Hyderabad-based DSPL went public in January at a market capitalisation of $32.9 million.
Skyroot Aerospace becomes Telangana’s latest unicorn
Telangana added one unicorn during the first nine months of 2026, compared with none in the corresponding period last year. Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace, which develops launch vehicles for small satellites, achieved unicorn status in May.
The number of new soonicorns, companies tracked by Tracxn as potential future unicorns, declined 67% to four from 12 in 9M 2025. Fortune India

November 24, 2026
Alameda, Calif.-based Science Corporation has raised $400 million in a Series D round, bringing its total funding to more than $900 million. Founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak, the company develops brain-computer interfaces, including PRIMA, a retinal implant designed to restore central vision in patients with advanced macular degeneration. The company will use the capital to expand PRIMA across Europe, prepare for U.S. regulatory approval, and advance its biohybrid neural interface research.
Science Corporation CEO Max Hodak.
Alameda, Calif.-based Science Corp . , a medical technology company developing brain-computer interfaces and neural technologies, has raised $400 million in a Series D financing round , bringing its total capital raised since its 2021 founding to more than $900 million. Investors participating in the round include Khosla Ventures, Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech , among others.
Founded in 2021 by Max Hodak , Science has built its initial commercial strategy around Prima, a retinal implant designed for patients with geographic atrophy caused by dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The condition damages the central retina and can significantly impair a person’s ability to recognize faces, read, and perform everyday activities. The company is also developing a biohybrid neural interface intended to establish more direct connections with the brain.
Hodak is an American biomedical engineer and serial entrepreneur with experience in biotechnology and brain-computer interfaces. He co-founded Neuralink with Elon Musk in 2016 and served as president until early 2021, during which he helped lead the development of implantable brain-machine interfaces.
Before Neuralink, he founded Transcriptic, a robotic cloud laboratory that enabled researchers to conduct biological experiments remotely through software. He also founded MyFit, a college admissions analytics platform that Naviance acquired in 2010.
Prima combines a photovoltaic implant placed beneath the retina with specially designed glasses. The glasses capture visual information and project it on to the implant using near-infrared light. The implant converts the light into electrical signals that stimulate retinal cells, allowing visual information to travel through the remaining visual pathway to the brain. The technology is being studied as a potential treatment for patients who have lost central vision because of geographic atrophy.
Science is also advancing its biohybrid architecture, which integrates engineered neurons into electronic devices rather than attempting to introduce conventional electronic components directly into the brain. According to the company, the architecture uses hundreds of thousands of neurons anchored to the device to establish connections with the brain at substantially higher bandwidth than current neural interfaces.
The company plans to use the capital to expand its availability across European markets and prepare for a U.S. launch, where it is pursuing approval through the Food and Drug Administration’s humanitarian device exemption pathway.
While investing in research, manufacturing, and operational infrastructure, Science is also advancing its biohybrid program and exploring potential applications of Prima in other retinal conditions, including Stargardt disease and retinitis pigmentosa.

candidates.title: Accel Leads a $277 Million Seed Round for Marlowe, Valuing the Non-Nvidia AI Inference Startup at $1.15 Billion
candidates.snippet: Accel Leads a $277 Million Seed Round for Marlowe, Valuing the Non-Nvidia AI Inference Startup at $1.15 Billion HedgeCo.Net
candidates.text:
Marlowe, an AI infrastructure startup founded in May by Convoy co-founder Dan Lewis and former Microsoft corporate vice president Kutta Srinivasan, has raised a $277 million seed round led by Accel. The financing values the company at $1.15 billion, according to the company as reported by GeekWire, making it a unicorn at the seed stage.
Marlowe said its seed investors include Accel, Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides, Eclipse, Journey, Valor, Emergence Capital, Pitango and Neo, among others. Quartz, citing Bloomberg, reported that Eclipse had led an earlier round and that Eclipse chief executive Lior Susan serves as Marlowe’s executive chairman. GeekWire noted angel backers including KKR co-founder Henry Kravis and Uber chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi.
The company is building what it calls multi-silicon AI factories: data centers designed specifically for inference workloads and built around chips from vendors other than Nvidia, starting with AMD and the startup Etched. Marlowe argues that co-designing chips, networking, power management and software can deliver two to three times more output per watt and per dollar than conventional GPU clouds. GeekWire reported that its first site, built around Etched chips, is scheduled to go live in December, with a larger AMD-based site targeted for the second quarter of 2027.
The size of the round reflects how capital-intensive AI infrastructure has become even at the earliest stage. The founders told GeekWire that much of the money will go toward chips, networking equipment and site operations, and that the company plans to prove its approach at sites of tens of megawatts before financing additional capacity site by site.
For venture investors, Marlowe is a bet that the shift from training models to running them will open room for alternatives to Nvidia’s dominant ecosystem. It also highlights a broader trend of seed rounds that look more like growth financings, which concentrates risk in fewer companies and raises the bar for follow-on rounds. Execution on the first two sites will be the key test of whether the valuation holds.

Chase Properties , a Beachwood, Ohio-based owner and operator of open-air shopping centers, and New York-based alternative asset manager Tru Arrow Partners have completed the final closings of two real estate investment funds, securing more than $148 million in combined capital commitments.
Tru Arrow-Chase Properties Partners (TACPP) closed at nearly $105 million, while Chase Properties Retail Opportunities Fund V closed at nearly $44 million. Both funds closed within their respective fundraising targets.
Fund V follows a core-plus investment strategy focused on stabilized, income-producing shopping centers, while TACPP pursues opportunistic investments across retail, multifamily and industrial properties, including investments alongside Chase Properties’ retail funds.

candidates.title: Avicena raises $100M to link AI chips with microLEDs instead of lasers
candidates.snippet: Avicena raises $100M to link AI chips with microLEDs instead of lasers The Next Web
candidates.text:
Avicena’s connectorised LightBundle microLED link, shown in September 2026
Credit: Avicena
Avicena, a Sunnyvale startup that links AI chips with tiny LEDs instead of lasers, has raised more than $100M in Series C funding. It also has a new chief executive. Kevin Pope succeeds Marco Chisari and will lead the company as it brings its first product to market next year.
InterVest led the round, Avicena announced on Tuesday. Other investors include Tiger Global, Cerberus Capital Management, SK hynix Ventures, Samsung Catalyst Fund and AMD Ventures. Prosperity7 Ventures, Mitsubishi Chemical’s Diamond Edge Ventures and Hitachi Ventures also took part. InterVest director John Dongwoo Ha joins Avicena’s board.
“AI infrastructure needs a new approach to moving data between accelerators, memory, and switches,” Pope said.
Light instead of copper
AI systems move ever more data between accelerators, memory and switches. Copper links face limits on reach, density and energy use, Avicena says. Memory bandwidth and capacity also increasingly hold systems back. SK hynix, one of the investors, has said the memory shortage will last until 2030.
Avicena’s LightBundle platform uses dense arrays of microLEDs and silicon photodetectors linked by multicore fibre. Rather than pushing a few channels very fast, it spreads data across many slower ones. That, the company says, cuts the need for data-rate conversion and complex signal processing.
Because it needs no lasers, the platform can sit close to compute and memory chips. Avicena pitches it for links inside and between chip packages, and across accelerator systems. By contrast, Photon Bridge raised $10M last month to build lasers for AI data centres.
From evaluation kits to a product
Avicena began shipping 1Tbps LightBundle evaluation kits in August. In September, it announced a version with connectors for the ECOC 2026 optics conference. It is meant to make assembly, testing and servicing easier.
The money will go on hiring, product development and engineering, Pope said. Two of the chipmakers behind the round see a role for the technology in memory.
“Energy-efficient optical interconnects are becoming increasingly important to next-generation memory architectures,” said SK hynix Ventures’ Rene Do.
SK hynix Ventures said it hopes to work with Avicena on future memory interconnects. Energy and data movement limit the AI build-out, said Samsung Catalyst Fund’s David Goldschmidt. AMD Ventures’ Patrick Rundell said moving data between compute, memory and networking chips is becoming critical.
Earlier this month, Marvell agreed to buy Lumentum , the Nvidia-backed optical component maker, in an all-stock deal.

China Physical AI Roundup: Simplexity Robotics Raises $100M Pre-A, Plus X Square Model, OYMotion and AgiBot Deployment
By Greg Bock · 24 November 2026 · 3 min read
AI Insider
Insider Brief
China’s physical AI sector saw new funding, robot technology releases and industrial deployments, alongside government efforts to develop national standards for embodied-intelligence data.
Simplexity Robotics raised $100 million at a $1.6 billion valuation and unveiled its iX wheeled humanoid, while OYMotion secured several hundred million yuan to expand its dexterous hand and robot training technology.
X Square Robot reported a 55.1% zero-shot success rate for its WALL-OSS-1.0 model across 312 real-robot tasks, while AgiBot began trial operations of its Genie G2 robots on a semiconductor testing line in Shanghai.
China ‘s physical AI industry continues to expand on several fronts, with fresh investment, advances in robotic intelligence and growing activity in industrial settings. This week’s developments also highlight specialized hardware, training data and emerging standards as companies work to move robots beyond demonstrations and into commercial use. Here’s a look at the latest developments.
Simplexity Robotics
Simplexity Robotics has raised $100 million in a pre-Series A round led by Ant Group at a $1.6 billion post-money valuation, Ifeng reported , citing chairman and co-founder Wang Kai. Wang made the comments in a Bloomberg interview and said Ant also joined as a strategic investor. TechNode , also citing Bloomberg, said existing investors Tencent, HSG and Lanchi Ventures participated as well and that the company was founded by former Li Auto executives.
Wang listed the company’s current backers as Vision Plus Capital, HSG, Lanchi Ventures, Tencent, Alibaba, Legend Capital, CAS Star and Gaorong Ventures, according to Ifeng. He said Lanchi, Tencent, Legend Capital and HSG have each invested in three or more rounds.
Simplexity also unveiled iX, its second humanoid and a wheeled robot that prepares and delivers drinks, fetches items and guides visitors, Ifeng said. Early customers include Korean robotics startup RLWRLD, Tsinghua University and forklift maker Hangcha Group. Simplexity has already put a warehouse sorting line into operation with Hangcha.
X Square Robot
X Square Robot introduced WALL-OSS-1.0, a vision-language-action foundation model for robots, the Shenzhen company announced . It reported a 55.1% zero-shot success rate across 312 real-robot tasks chosen by evaluators, with no task-specific training. On ManipArena, a real-world benchmark of 15 tabletop tasks, the model scored 1,101 out of 1,500 points without task-specific fine-tuning, 70.8% higher than a fine-tuned π0.5 baseline, according to the company.
X Square said a compact Nano version of the model ran 18 robots on one Nvidia Blackwell GPU in a tested configuration. It also said a WALL-OSS-1.0-based parcel-sorting policy for an unnamed logistics customer kept more than 90% of its original-site speed and success rate when moved across sites. The company said it will open-source the model’s weights soon.
OYMotion
OYMotion , a Shanghai maker of dexterous robot hands and muscle-signal technology, has closed a Series D of several hundred million yuan, 36Kr reported in an exclusive, citing the company. The exact amount was undisclosed. Zhongbing Shunjing, Changjiang Capital and Guanggu Industrial Investment invested in the round, OYMotion’s second this year after a 150 million yuan (about $22 million) Series C in March. It is also preparing to list.
According to the company, OYMotion supplies nearly 200 embodied-AI firms and runs a Zhuhai plant with annual capacity of more than 10,000 units. OYMotion offers EMG-EGO, a wristband system that records muscle signals, hand motion and object data for robot training. Proceeds will go to commercializing its embodied-AI business, 36Kr said, citing vice president Zhang Qi.
AgiBot
AgiBot ‘s first batch of Genie G2 robots has entered trial operation on a chip-test line at JCET’s automotive-electronics plant in Lingang, Shanghai, Xinmin Evening News reported . The robots load trays of chips awaiting test, unload tested trays and sort good from bad parts with no human help, the report said. The unit count was undisclosed. The G2 connects to JCET’s existing manufacturing execution and equipment automation systems, and the two companies plan to jointly validate more packaging and test steps.
National Data Administration
China’s National Data Administration has begun drafting national standards for embodied-intelligence data, CCTV reported , citing the agency. During the 15th Five-Year Plan period, from 2026 to 2030, it expects to issue more than 20 dedicated national standards and to run pilot validation at the same time. CCTV said the work will support deployments of humanoid robots, special-purpose robots and industrial collaborative arms.

Harbinger has secured more than $100 million in financing from Erebor Bank and Pinegrove Venture Partners to accelerate production and support its growing commercial vehicle business.

Its private credit strategy provides financing solutions to growth-stage companies, including businesses with significant capital requirements. Zipher raised $53 million to automate cloud capacity decisions that data teams now make manually in advance.
Hertz cut compute costs by 25% to 40% while holding performance steady through seasonal peaks with Zipher.
Zipher's execution layer targets performance and budget goals rather than simply choosing the cheapest infrastructure.
Zipher has raised $53 million across its seed and Series A rounds to automate how enterprise data workloads run in the cloud. The company said TLV Partners , Maor Investments and Glilot Capital backed the rounds. It did not disclose how much each round contributed or the valuation.
The funding will go toward research and development and expanding sales, including a larger U.S. enterprise sales operation and growth outside the United States. Founded in 2024 by CEO Dan Coster and CTO Yoav Gill Ben Ephraim, Zipher targets the infrastructure underneath analytics and AI projects: the computing resources that move, transform and process data before people or applications use it.
How Zipher Allocates Cloud Capacity
Data teams have traditionally chosen cluster configurations, job schedules and execution engines ahead of time. That works when a job’s input volume and deadline are reasonably predictable. But a pipeline that processes steady traffic on most days might need considerably more memory during a holiday rush or when a backlog lands. Reserving enough capacity for the largest run can waste money on quiet days; sizing every run for the average can make an unexpectedly large job miss its deadline.
Zipher’s product documentation describes an execution layer that learns from earlier runs, looks for recurring changes in demand and adjusts resources accordingly. Customers define targets such as how quickly a job must finish and how much it should cost. Zipher says its software can then adjust a cluster, route a workload to another engine or rewrite it for another framework. The company lists support for workloads on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud and integrations with tools including Apache Airflow, dbt and Databricks Workflows.
One example is deciding when a job can use spare cloud capacity. Amazon EC2 Spot Instances use capacity that AWS can reclaim. That can make them a fit for work that can recover from an interruption, but a poor fit when interruption would put a deadline at risk. Zipher says it monitors spot availability and can adjust resources if capacity is reclaimed or a job runs out of memory. The point is not to use the cheapest infrastructure on every run. It is to weigh the cost of that run against the cost of an interruption or missed deadline.
What the Customer Results Show
Hertz uses Zipher for production data workloads, according to the announcement. Gaurav Rastogi, Hertz’s senior director of enterprise data analytics and BI platforms, said in a statement distributed by Zipher that the rental company saw compute costs fall by 25% to 40%, depending on the workload, while maintaining consistent performance during seasonal peaks. Zipher does not disclose a common baseline across customers or separate the effect of its various optimizations, so the Hertz figures illustrate one deployment rather than a savings target for every buyer.
The company has also published case studies on how customers such as SciPlay and Yotpo use its execution layer. Those examples give potential buyers places to start evaluating fit, but they do not replace a trial that accounts for their own data volumes, cloud contracts and recovery requirements.
The rise of agent-generated workloads adds a new dimension to the operational demands of agentic AI infrastructure . Creating another pipeline can be easy; keeping the expanding collection on time and within budget remains an infrastructure problem. Zipher’s approach places those execution decisions in an autonomous layer, with performance targets and budgets defining the outcome it is meant to deliver.
That makes the full cost and reliability of a completed workload more important than the price of a single compute instance. Retries, data transfers and missed deadlines all affect the result. Zipher’s funding will support its effort to bring that operating model to more enterprise environments.

University Of Pennsylvania Receives $15 Million Commitment From Josh And Marjorie Harris
Josh Harris and his wife, Marjorie Harris, have made a $15 million commitment to the University of Pennsylvania through Harris Philanthropies.
The commitment includes $10 million to establish the Harris Family Alternative Investments Center at the Wharton School and $5 million to renovate Penn Wrestling’s facilities and support the athletic program.
The gifts, announced during Josh Harris’ 40th Wharton reunion, bring the couple’s total support for the university to approximately $34 million. Their cumulative giving to Wharton’s alternative-investments programming now totals $25 million.
Expanding Alternative Investments Research
The $10 million Wharton gift will transform the Harris Alternative Investments Program into the Harris Family Alternative Investments Center.
Harris originally established the program in 2019 with a $10 million commitment. The new center will expand its work across student programming, faculty research and engagement with the global investment industry.
Its research will examine how private markets are evolving and how their growth affects institutions, investors and beneficiaries. The center also plans to translate academic findings into practical industry insights and policy recommendations.
The existing Wharton Alternative Investments Summit will become the Harris Family Alternative Investments Conference. The event will convene investment professionals, academics, alumni and students to discuss trends shaping private equity and other alternative asset classes.
Fellowships And Financial Data
Harris Student Fellows will receive stipends, funding for travel and invitations to center events. They will also gain access to affiliated faculty, guest speakers, industry executives and professional mentors.
The center will establish a dedicated data hub offering premium financial datasets to Wharton students, faculty members and researchers studying alternative investments and private markets.
The commitment also expands Harris’ previous support for the Wharton Private Equity Professorship, held by Bilge Yilmaz, and the Joshua J. Harris Professorship, held by Thomas S. Robertson.
Yilmaz and Burcu Esmer will serve as the center’s academic directors.
New Penn Wrestling Facilities
The Harrises’ $5 million athletics gift will support the renovation of Weightman Hall and the creation of the Pottruck-Reina Wrestling Center.
The 13,000-square-foot project will include the 8,900-square-foot Harris Family Wrestling Room, which will serve as the team’s main training space. A new 2,400-square-foot team complex will replace the adjacent Donaldson Room and provide athletes with modern locker rooms and related facilities.
The renovated center is expected to open in spring 2028.
Part of the gift will support the Grapplers Fund, which gives Penn Wrestling flexible resources for program operations. The commitment builds on Harris’ prior support for coaching, recruiting, team travel, nutrition and equipment.
Harris competed as a wrestler while attending Penn. The National Wrestling Hall of Fame recognized him as an Outstanding American in 2013.

Pai Defence , a British-Ukrainian defense tech startup, has raised $5 million (€4.58 million) in pre-seed funding to expand its network of drone detection sensors in Ukraine and further develop its machine-learning software. Nordic venture capital fund Gardar led the round.
UA1, D3, Green Flag, Defence Builder, 1991 Ventures, Motanka, WildField, TA Ventures, and Angel One also participated.

An alert can tell a unit that a drone is nearby. Pai’s aim is to bring those detections together so units can see how drone activity changes over time.
“For the most lethal weapon on the frontline, a detector’s beep when the drone is almost overhead is far too late,” said Zakorchemna, Pai Defence’s CEO and co-founder.
The company says it has tested its system in combat with Ukrainian military units and tracked more than 100,000 drone flights . It is using that data to refine its software as drone activity and tactics change.
“We believe Pai Defence has cracked the code for a major part of this problem, and that they can contribute to saving many lives on the frontlines,” said Erlend Prestgard, Gardar Managing Partner.

Inside a large financial institution, “integration work quietly eats the roadmap, and insurers pay that cost again every time they onboard an employer,” according to Gaurav Kapoor, General Partner at Diagram.
“[Eight by Zero] does that work once and keeps it running, so carriers can put their people on claims and coverage,” he remarked.
Eight by Zero represents an “opportunity to create a more connected experience for our plan sponsors and advisors,” believes Julia McGillis, Executive Vice President of Workplace Benefits & Retirement at Canada Life.
“The capabilities developed by Eight by Zero will further accelerate investments we’re making in technology to simplify how data is connected across benefits and insurance, helping reduce integration complexity for employers and carriers,” she commented.
Proceeds from the seed round will fund product development, expansion into new lines of coverage, customer implementation capacity, and commercial growth, according to a statement from the Canadian fintech.
Eight by Zero was founded in 2025.

ETtech (L-R) Abhinav Garg, Himanshu Agrawal, Puneet Sharma and Gaurav Mittal, founders, Vegapay
Amsterdam-listed technology investor Prosus is set to lead a Rs 38.4 crore funding round in fintech infrastructure startup Vegapay , with participation from existing investors Elevation Capital, Vertex Ventures and Eximius Ventures.
Prosus will invest Rs 28.8 crore through its investment arm, while Elevation Capital, Vertex Ventures and Eximius Ventures will put in Rs 6 crore, Rs 2.3 crore and Rs 1.3 crore, respectively, according to filings with the Registrar of Companies.
The investment will value the Mumbai-based startup at about Rs 380 crore ($38-40 million) post-money, according to the share issuance details. Prosus will hold a 7.6% stake in the company, while Elevation Capital will own 25.1%.
The proposed investment comes just months after Vegapay raised Rs 37.9 crore from its existing investors in a round led by Vertex Ventures. People aware of the matter said the latest share issuance is part of a larger funding round. Entrackr first reported the proposed share issuance.
The deal marks an expansion of Prosus' fintech investment portfolio beyond companies directly offering credit and other financial products to those building the underlying technology infrastructure for financial institutions.
ET reported earlier this month that Prosus, which has invested $100 million in the Sachin Bansal-founded Navi, around $80 million in supply-chain financing platform Mintifi and $100 million in Vastu Housing Finance over the past two years, is looking to increase its exposure to financial services after years of backing consumer internet companies in India.
“You will see us over-indexing on financial services,” Ashutosh Sharma, head of India investments at Prosus, had told ET, pointing to opportunities where technology can expand access to financial products or improve the economics of delivering them.
Prosus was also close to investing in artificial intelligence-led credit management startup Oolka, ET had reported.
Founded in 2022 by Gaurav Mittal, Himanshu Agrawal, Puneet Sharma and Abhinav Garg, Vegapay develops software for banks and non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) to launch and manage credit products without having to overhaul their existing technology systems.
Its offerings include card issuance and management, credit lines on the Unified Payments Interface (UPI), as well as software for loan origination, colending and collections. It competes with rivals such as SoftBank-backed banking technology startup Zeta.
Vegapay had raised $5.5 million in May 2024 in a round led by Elevation Capital. Its operating revenue grew nearly threefold to Rs 8.7 crore in FY26, while the net loss widened marginally to Rs 18.7 crore.
